title: Tria capita ex opere quodam majori inedito de theoria lunae

deep.reconstruction:
Problem served: using the timed contacts of a lunar eclipse to correct the position of the lunar node (and so the node tables), and then the inclination.

Setting (continuing from §14-15):
- m, n are the hourly motions of the Sun (so of the shadow centre) and of the Moon; k is the hourly retrograde motion of the node. Relative to the node, the shadow centre moves at m+k and the Moon at n+k per hour.
- At mid-eclipse the shadow centre is at σ and the Moon's centre at λ, with arcs ☊σ = x and ☊λ = y.
- The 'reduction' x − y = U − L = c = (m+n+2k) sin 2x tan²(ρ/2) / (g(n−m)). Since sin 2x and ρ are roughly known, Euler treats c as given.

The end of §15 (top of the page) notes two things. Neglecting the angle η costs only a few seconds of arc. Any pair of symmetric phases (first/last contact, immersion/emersion, equal phases with LS = ls) yields the same mid-eclipse moment.

§16: L, S are the positions of Moon and shadow centre at first contact, and l, s at last contact. Then SL = sl = f, the sum of the apparent semidiameters. With h the duration in hours, Lλ = lλ = ½h(n+k) and Sσ = σs = ½h(m+k). Hence ☊L = x − ½h(n+k) − c and ☊S = x − ½h(m+k).

§17: Put a = ½h(n+k) and b = ½h(m+k). Spherical triangle S☊L has sides P = ☊L = x−a−c, Q = ☊S = x−b, SL = f, and angle ρ at the node. The cosine rule gives cos f = cos ρ sin P sin Q + cos P cos Q. Writing cos ρ = 1 − 2 sin²(ρ/2) and using product formulas:
  cos f = cos²(ρ/2) cos(P−Q) + sin²(ρ/2) cos(P+Q),
i.e. cos(2x−a−b−c) = [cos f − cos²(ρ/2) cos(a−b+c)] / sin²(ρ/2).

Triangle l☊s has ☊l = x−c+a and ☊s = x+b, giving
  cos(2x+a+b−c) = [cos f − cos²(ρ/2) cos(a−b−c)] / sin²(ρ/2).

Dividing the two eliminates sin²(ρ/2), the factor most sensitive to errors in ρ. Expanding with T = tan(2x−c) gives
  [cos(a+b) + sin(a+b)T] / [cos(a+b) − sin(a+b)T] = N/D,
hence
  tan(2x−c) = sin(a−b) cos(a+b) sin c cos²(ρ/2) / [sin(a+b)(cos f − cos(a−b) cos c cos²(ρ/2))].

§18: The residual error in ρ is harmless through cos²(ρ/2). But the result is proportional to sin c, a tiny and uncertain quantity, so 2x−c is badly determined. In other words, a single pair of symmetric contacts carries information on the node only through the second-order asymmetry c. This motivates §18-19 (next page), which combine the outer contacts with immersion/emersion in total eclipses.
errors: No mathematical errors found: both cosine-rule reductions and the final tan(2x−c) formula check out algebraically (N−D = 2cos²(ρ/2) sin(a−b) sin c; N+D = 2cos f − 2cos²(ρ/2) cos(a−b) cos c).

Implicit circularity: c itself contains sin 2x (and tan²(ρ/2)), yet it is treated as known ('pro dato'). This is acceptable for iterative correction of an approximately known node, but not stated explicitly. In the small-angle limit, substituting c ∝ sin 2x makes the equation essentially one for cos 2x, a further sign of the ill-conditioning Euler diagnoses.
The denominator cos f − cos²(ρ/2) cos(a−b) cos c is itself a small difference of order sin²(ρ/2) − f²/2 + (a−b)²/2. So the conditioning is worse than Euler's remark about c alone suggests.

ideas.what: Reducing contact timings of a lunar eclipse to two spherical triangles at the node, giving cos(2x∓…) in terms of f and ρ via the half-angle form of the spherical cosine rule
ideas.modern_name: Determination of orbital node from eclipse contact timings (orbit determination by spherical trigonometry)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical practice (Ptolemy onward; 18th-c. lunar theorists such as Mayer and Euler)
ideas.where_published: E838 Opera postuma 1862; similar eclipse-based node and inclination determinations appear in 18th-c. lunar literature

ideas.what: Dividing the two equations to eliminate sin²(ρ/2), the error-sensitive factor in the inclination
ideas.modern_name: Eliminating an ill-determined nuisance parameter by ratios

ideas.what: Recognition that the node solution from one symmetric pair of contacts is proportional to the small asymmetry c, hence ill-conditioned; this motivates combining two different chord pairs (outer and inner contacts)
ideas.modern_name: Error propagation / ill-conditioning analysis in parameter estimation
ideas.usually_credited_to: General 18th-c. error-awareness; formal theory with Gauss and Legendre

missed.claim: Euler gives an explicit sensitivity diagnosis: a single pair of symmetric eclipse contacts determines the node only through the tiny second-order reduction term c. He therefore proposes using two chord lengths (outer contacts and immersion/emersion) to separate node and inclination. This is a small but clear instance of pre-least-squares conditioning analysis in observational astronomy. It is likely known to editors of the Opera postuma lunar material, but rarely discussed.

deep.surprise_reason: Correct, routine spherical-trigonometric reduction for eclipse-based node determination. The only noteworthy feature is the explicit conditioning remark, which is natural for the time.
